question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Types of Images Formed by an Affine Transformation
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/c36f3eb07b45eebf7f4de2a26cb366ca4ab785b5c7e8e6d25eb7bbad2c418838.png)

Consider the affine transformation $T,$ given by

$$
x=3u-v-1,\,y=2u+5v.
$$

What would be the image of the rectangle shown above under the action of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

The given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u-v-1 \\ 2u+5v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u-v \\ 2u+5v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}].$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot 5-2\cdot (-1) \\  & =17 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a non-singular matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is invertible, and the image of the rectangle under the action of $T$ is a parallelogram.

provenance.kp_title: Identifying the Types of Images Formed by an Affine Transformation

Consider the set $A,$ shown above. The boundary of $A$ is given by

$$
∂A=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,\,\}.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097897/assets/d1946cea37f202705e6517ba760afa6617075f748901b10588ea98628a3e9e50.png)

Therefore, 

$$
∂A=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,2y={x}^{2}\,\}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Interior of a Set
question.problem:

Consider the set $A$ shown above. The interior of $A$ is 

$$
\text{int}\,A=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0<x<3,\,\}.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097897/assets/c0e6ef400b15c54264a400af99bef64c3bb5aeb7ceadbdd599375c0f1e0d3642.png)

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

The interior of $A$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097897/assets/8c5bbdfca6736194791f834ab4aadb03a30e3f116e89ffd5a7ea3e0104708ae4.png)

So, in this case, the interior of $A$ is given by

$$
\text{int}\,A=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0<x<3,\,0<y<\frac{2}{3}x\}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Displacement of a Particle Given Its Velocity
question.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t$ is given by $v(t)=2t-\sqrt{t}.$ What is the total displacement of the particle between $t=0$ and $t=9?$
question.worked_solution:
We find the total displacement by calculating the definite integral of the velocity.

Let $d$ be the total displacement. Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={\int }_{0}^{9}(2t-\sqrt{t})\text{d}t \\  & ={({t}^{2}-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2})|}_{0}^{9} \\  & =[(9)^{2}-\frac{2}{3}(9)^{3/2}]-[(0)^{2}-\frac{2}{3}(0)^{3/2}] \\  & =81-18-0 \\  & =63.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the total displacement between $t=0$ and $t=9$ is $63.$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Total Displacement of a Particle Given Its Velocity

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
question.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)={e}^{2-t}.$ At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=e.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=2?$
question.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=2$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,2].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(2)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{2}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =e+{\int }_{1}^{2}{e}^{2-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =e+{[-{e}^{2-t}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =e+([-{e}^{2-2}]-[-{e}^{2-1}]) \\  & =e+([-{e}^{0}]-[-{e}^{1}]) \\  & =e+(-1+e) \\  & =2e-1\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=2$ is $x=2e-1.$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Final Position of a Particle

question.knowledge_point: Identifying Open and Closed Sets of Real Numbers
question.problem:
Which of the following sets are closed?

I. $[-2,2]$

II. $[3,9]$

III. $[-1,1)\cup (3,4]$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Among the given sets, only $[-2,2]$ and $[3,9]$ are closed because:

- The boundary points of $[-2,2]$ are $-2$, and $2.$ Both of them lie in the set.

- The boundary points of $[3,9]$ are $3$, and $9.$ Both of them lie in the set.

The other set is not closed because $[-1,1)\cup (3,4]$ has a boundary point $1$, which does not lie in the set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

provenance.kp_title: Identifying Open and Closed Sets of Real Numbers

question.knowledge_point: Identifying Open and Closed Sets of Real Numbers
question.problem:
Which of the following sets are closed?

I. $(6,10]$

II. $[2,5]$

III. $[0,1]\cup [3,4]$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Among the given sets, only $[2,5]$ and $[0,1]\cup [3,4]$ are closed because:

- The boundary points of $[2,5]$ are $2$ and $5.$ Both of them lie in the set.

- The boundary points of $[0,1]\cup [3,4]$ are $0,1,3,$ and $4.$ All of them lie in the set.

The other set is not closed because $(6,10]$ has a boundary point $6$, which does not lie in the set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only".

question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Angles and Magnitudes
question.problem: Suppose $|\,p\,|=2$ and the angle between vectors $p$ and $q$ is $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{6}.$ Find the scalar projection of $p$ onto $q.$
question.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{q}\,p & =|\,p\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Angles and Magnitudes

question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Components
question.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 6+(-1)\cdot 2+2\cdot (-3)}{\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{49}} \\  & =\frac{4}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{b\cdot a}{|\,a\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{a}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{a}_{x}^{2}+{a}_{y}^{2}+{a}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a-{\text{comp}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{4}{7}-\frac{4}{3} \\  & =4(\frac{1}{7}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =4(\frac{3}{21}-\frac{7}{21}) \\  & =-\frac{16}{21}.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Components

question.knowledge_point: Projecting a Vector Onto a Perpendicular Vector
question.problem: Let $p=i+2j+xk$ and $q=3i+6j-3k.$ Given that the scalar projection of $p$ onto $q$ is zero, find the value of $x.$
question.worked_solution:
Since $p$ is a nonzero vector, its scalar projection onto another nonzero vector $q$ equals zero only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
p⊥q\,⟹\,p\cdot q=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & ={p}_{x}\cdot {q}_{x}+{p}_{y}\cdot {q}_{y}+{p}_{z}\cdot {q}_{z} \\  & =1\cdot 3+2\cdot 6+x\cdot (-3) \\  & =15-3x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot q & =0 \\ 15-3x & =0 \\ 3x & =15 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Projecting a Vector Onto a Perpendicular Vector

question.knowledge_point: Solving a Singular 2x2 System of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination
question.problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-6y=2 \\ -4x+24y=-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system.
question.worked_solution:
First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 & 2 \\ -4 & 24 & -10\end{aligned}]
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 & 2 \\ -4 & 24 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-6y=2 \\ 0x+0y=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

However, the final equation $0x+0y=-2$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=-2,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

provenance.kp_title: Solving a Singular 2x2 System of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination

question.knowledge_point: Reducing an Augmented Matrix for a Singular 2x2 System to REF and Solving the Resulting System
question.problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form.
question.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
The function $f(x,y)$ is defined as 

$$
f(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.
$$

Evaluate this function at the point $(-6,-\frac{\pi }{4}).$
question.worked_solution:
To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(-6,-\frac{\pi }{4}),$ we substitute $x=-6$ and $y=-\frac{\pi }{4}$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-6,-\frac{\pi }{4}) & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,{|}_{(-6,-\pi /4)} \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-6(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(3,{e}^{2}),$ we substitute $x=3$ and $y={e}^{2}$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{|}_{(3,{e}^{2})} & =(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-1){|}_{(3,{e}^{2})} \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})-1 \\  & =3(2\operatorname{ln}⁡e)-1 \\  & =3(2)-1 \\  & =6-1 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$
